lessons.title: Your first web page
lessons.topic: Understanding HTML structure and basic tags
lessons.big: A web page is like a house. HTML is the walls and rooms. Every page has the same frame: a head (the name tag on the door) and a body (everything people see inside).
lessons.analogy: Think of a letter: the head is the envelope (title, who it is for), the body is the letter itself.
steps: Every page starts with <!DOCTYPE html>. It tells the phone: this is a modern web page.
<html> wraps everything. Inside it are two parts: <head> and <body>.
<title> goes in the head. It shows on the browser tab.

is the biggest heading.

is a paragraph. Most tags open

and close

with a slash.

lessons.title: Colour and style with CSS
lessons.topic: Basic CSS styling and formatting
lessons.big: HTML is the house. CSS is the paint, the curtains and the furniture. CSS says: "pick this thing, then change how it looks".
lessons.analogy: A CSS rule is like telling a tailor: "for every shirt (selector), make the colour green (property: value)".
steps: A rule looks like this: h1 { color: green; }
selector = who to style (h1, p, body). property = what to change (color). value = how (green).
A class lets you style some things only. In HTML: class="price". In CSS: .price { }
Colours can be names (green), or hex codes like #1f7a3a.

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.topic: Advanced CSS: box model and positioning
lessons.big: Every thing on a web page is a box. A box has content in the middle, padding (space inside), a border (the edge) and margin (space outside).
lessons.analogy: Think of a gift in a box: the gift is the content, the soft paper is padding, the box wall is the border, and the gap to the next gift on the shelf is the margin.
steps: padding = space INSIDE the border. margin = space OUTSIDE it.
border: 2px solid green; draws the edge.
border-radius: 12px; rounds the corners.
position: relative on the card, and position: absolute on the badge, lets the badge sit in a corner of the card.

lessons.title: A page that fits any phone
lessons.topic: Responsive design basics
lessons.big: Your page will be opened on tiny phones and big screens. Responsive means the page bends to fit, like water in a bowl.
lessons.analogy: A responsive page is like a wrapper cloth (wrapper): it fits whoever wears it.
steps: The viewport meta tag tells phones: use the real screen width. Without it, the page looks tiny.
display: flex puts boxes in a row. flex-wrap: wrap lets them go to the next line when there is no space.
max-width: 100% on images stops pictures from sticking out of the screen.
Use flexible sizes (flex: 1 1 200px) instead of fixed widths.

quiz.q: What does flex-wrap: wrap do?

quiz.q: Why add max-width: 100% to images?
o: So they never stick out of the screen
quiz.why: The picture shrinks to fit its container.

lessons.title: Media queries: one page, many screens
lessons.topic: Responsive design basics with media queries
lessons.big: A media query is an IF for CSS: "IF the screen is at least 600px wide, THEN use these rules". On a phone you get the simple layout. On a big screen you get more.
lessons.analogy: It is like a wrapper cloth you tie one way for work and another way for church. Same cloth, different look for a different place.
steps: Start with the PHONE layout first. This is called mobile-first.
@media (min-width: 600px) { ... } means: only when the screen is 600px or wider.
Inside the curly braces, write normal CSS rules.
You can change many things: direction, font size, number of columns.

quiz.q: What is "mobile-first"?

lessons.title: Forms: asking questions
lessons.topic: HTML forms and input handling
lessons.big: A form is how a page asks questions and collects answers. Every question has a label (the words) and an input (the box where people answer).
lessons.analogy: A form is like the register at school: each line has a name tag (label) and a space to write (input).
steps: <form> wraps all the questions.
<label for="name"> and <input id="name"> are joined when for and id match. Tapping the label then opens the box. This also helps screen readers.
<select> with <option> items gives a drop-down list.
<textarea> is a big box for long text. <button type="submit"> sends the form.

required means: the form will not send until this box is filled.
type="email" and type="number" with min and max make the browser check the answer.

lessons.big: HTML is the structure. CSS is the style. JavaScript is the BRAIN: it makes the page react when someone taps, types or scrolls.
lessons.analogy: HTML is the house, CSS is the paint, JavaScript is the electricity. Press the switch (event) and the light (page) responds.
steps: <script> holds JavaScript. Put it at the bottom of the <body>.
document.getElementById("btn") finds an element by its id.
addEventListener("click", function () { ... }) means: when this is tapped, run this code.
textContent changes the words. let count = 0; makes a variable (a box that remembers a number).

lessons.title: Variables: boxes with names
lessons.topic: Basic syntax, variables, and data types
lessons.big: A variable is a labelled box that remembers something. You give the box a name and put a value inside. Later you can use the name to get the value back.
lessons.analogy: A variable is like a bottle with a label "Palm oil". You do not need to see inside every time, you just read the label.
steps: const makes a box that never changes. let makes a box you can change later.
Text goes in quotes: "Ade". Numbers have no quotes: 500. true and false are booleans.
console.log(thing) prints it in the Console below your code.
Backticks let you mix text and variables: `Welcome to ${shopName}!`

quiz.q: Which one can be changed later?
quiz.why: const is constant: it never changes. let can change.

quiz.q: Which is a number?
quiz.why: Anything in quotes is text, even if it looks like a number.

quiz.q: What does console.log(x) do?

lessons.title: Numbers, text and maths
lessons.topic: Basic syntax, variables, and data types
lessons.big: Computers are great at maths. JavaScript does + - * / for numbers. But careful: the + sign joins TEXT and adds NUMBERS. "5" + 3 is "53", not 8!
lessons.analogy: If you write 5 on a paper (text) it is just a drawing. If you hold 5 naira (number) you can count with it.
steps: + - * / and % (remainder) work on numbers.
"5" is text. Number("5") turns it into the number 5.
.toFixed(2) rounds a number to 2 decimal places and gives text.
typeof x tells you if x is a "number", "string" (text) or "boolean".

quiz.q: What does "5" + 3 give in JavaScript?
quiz.why: When one side is text, + joins them.

quiz.q: How do you turn the text "7" into a number?
quiz.why: Number() converts text to a number.

quiz.q: What does the % sign do?
quiz.why: 7 % 3 is 1 because 3 goes into 7 twice with 1 left.

lessons.title: Decide and repeat
lessons.topic: Conditional statements and loops
lessons.big: Two superpowers: DECIDE (if / else) and REPEAT (loops). With them your code can make choices and do boring work again and again without getting tired.
lessons.analogy: If: "If it is raining, take an umbrella, else wear a cap." Loop: "Sweep the floor 5 times."
steps: if (condition) { ... } else { ... } runs one block or the other.
=== means "is exactly equal". >= means "bigger or equal". && means AND. || means OR.
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { ... } repeats 5 times. i counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
while (condition) { ... } repeats as long as the condition is true. Make sure something changes or it never stops!

missions.say: Use if / else: when qty is 5 or more, discount must become 10.
Print "Big order!" when qty >= 5 (else "Small order").
Use a for loop to print 1 x 2 = 2 up to 5 x 2 = 10.
missions.hint: for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { console.log(i + " x 2 = " + i * 2); }

missions.say: Use a while loop: print 3, 2, 1 and then "Go!".

quiz.q: What does === mean?
quiz.why: One = puts a value in a box. Three === asks if two things are the same.

quiz.q: for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) runs how many times?
quiz.why: i is 1, then 2, then 3. After that i <= 3 is false.

quiz.q: What is dangerous in a while loop?
o: Nothing changes inside, so it never stops
quiz.why: An infinite loop freezes the page. Always change the counter.

lessons.title: Functions: your own tools
lessons.topic: Functions and scope
lessons.big: A function is a recipe you write once and use many times. You give it ingredients (parameters), it does the work and hands back the result (return).
lessons.analogy: A function is like a puff-puff machine: put in flour and sugar, it gives out puff-puff. Use it 100 times without rebuilding it.
steps: function total(price, qty) { return price * qty; } makes the tool.
total(250, 4) uses the tool. The answer comes back.

lessons.title: Touch the page: the DOM
lessons.topic: DOM manipulation
lessons.big: The browser turns your HTML into a tree of objects called the DOM. JavaScript can find any piece, change its words, its colours, even build new pieces from nothing.
lessons.analogy: Your page is a wall with photo frames. The DOM lets JavaScript swap a photo, repaint a frame or hang a new one.
steps: document.getElementById("title") finds one element.
element.textContent = "..." changes the words. element.style.color = "green" changes colour.
document.createElement("li") makes a new element. list.appendChild(li) puts it on the page.
element.classList.add("highlight") adds a CSS class.

quiz.q: Which line changes the words of an element?
quiz.why: textContent sets the words.

quiz.q: What does appendChild do?
o: Puts a new element on the page
quiz.why: A new element does not show until you append it.

lessons.title: PHP: your first script
lessons.topic: Basic PHP syntax and variables
lessons.big: PHP is a language that runs on the server (the computer that serves websites) and prepares the page BEFORE it reaches your phone. Facebook, Wikipedia and many Nigerian websites use it. PHP runs on a SERVER, not on your phone. In this lab a small PHP practice runner in your browser runs your code, so you can learn the basics. It supports the beginner parts of PHP.
lessons.analogy: JavaScript works in the customer's hands (the browser). PHP works in the kitchen (the server) and sends out the food ready.
steps: PHP code lives between <?php and ?>. Every line ends with a semicolon ;
Variables start with a dollar sign: $shop = "Mama T";
echo prints something. Join text with a dot: "Hi " . $name
\n starts a new line inside double quotes.

quiz.why: The dollar sign marks a variable: $price.

quiz.q: How do you join text in PHP?
quiz.why: In PHP the dot joins text. The plus is for adding numbers.

quiz.q: Where does PHP run?
quiz.why: The server runs PHP, then sends the finished page.

lessons.title: PHP: arrays and types
lessons.topic: Basic PHP syntax and variables
lessons.big: An array is ONE variable that holds MANY things, like a shopping list. A list can have numbers (0, 1, 2…) or names (like "Tomatoes") for each slot. PHP runs on a SERVER, not on your phone. In this lab a small PHP practice runner in your browser runs your code, so you can learn the basics. It supports the beginner parts of PHP.
lessons.analogy: An array is a tray of drinks: each place on the tray holds one bottle, and you can point to a place by its number or its label.
steps: $items = ["Tomatoes", "Rice"]; The first one is $items[0] (counting starts at 0).
count($items) tells you how many.
$prices = ["Rice" => 300]; has labels. Read it with $prices["Rice"].
$items[] = "Yam"; adds one to the end. strlen("Ade") counts letters. strtoupper("ade") makes capitals.

lessons.title: PHP: decide and repeat
lessons.topic: Control structures and functions in PHP
lessons.big: The same two superpowers you used in JavaScript, now in PHP: if / elseif / else to decide, and for / foreach to repeat. foreach is special: it walks through every item in a list. PHP runs on a SERVER, not on your phone. In this lab a small PHP practice runner in your browser runs your code, so you can learn the basics. It supports the beginner parts of PHP.
lessons.analogy: foreach is like a teacher calling the register: "next name, next name, next name" until the list ends.
steps: foreach ($prices as $name => $cost) { ... } gives you each label and value.
for ($i = 1; $i <= 3; $i++) { ... } counts for you.
$total += $cost; adds to a running total (it is short for $total = $total + $cost).
lessons.starter:
<?php
$prices = ["{{I1}}" => {{P1n}}, "{{I2}}" => {{P2n}}, "{{I3}}" => {{P3n}}];
$qty = 6;

// Mission 1: if $qty >= 10 echo "Big order!", elseif $qty >= 5 echo "Medium order", else "Small order"
// Mission 2: foreach: echo each line like this:  Name - ₦price   (one per line)
// Mission 3: a for loop that echoes "Day 1", "Day 2", "Day 3" (each on its own line)
// Mission 4: use foreach and += to find the total of all prices. Echo "Total: ₦" and the number
lessons.solution:
<?php
$prices = ["{{I1}}" => {{P1n}}, "{{I2}}" => {{P2n}}, "{{I3}}" => {{P3n}}];
$qty = 6;

if ($qty >= 10) {
  echo "Big order!\n";
} elseif ($qty >= 5) {
  echo "Medium order\n";
} else {
  echo "Small order\n";
}

foreach ($prices as $name => $cost) {
  echo $name . " - ₦" . $cost . "\n";
}

for ($day = 1; $day <= 3; $day++) {
  echo "Day " . $day . "\n";
}

$total = 0;
foreach ($prices as $cost) {
  $total += $cost;
}
echo "Total: ₦" . $total . "\n";

missions.say: Use if / elseif / else: with $qty = 6 it must echo "Medium order".
Use foreach to echo each line as: Name - ₦price
Use a for loop to echo Day 1, Day 2, Day 3.
Find the total with foreach and += then echo "Total: ₦" and the number.

lessons.turn: Add a fourth price. Run it again: does your total update by itself? That is the power of a loop.

quiz.q: What does foreach do?
o: Walks through every item in a list
quiz.why: foreach gives you each item one by one.

quiz.q: $total += 5;  means…
quiz.why: += adds to what is already there.

quiz.q: In PHP, which word means "otherwise if"?
quiz.why: PHP uses elseif (or else if).

lessons.title: Project: the PHP receipt machine
lessons.topic: Control structures and functions in PHP
lessons.big: Your last project. Write PHP functions that print a receipt for your stall. A function is a tool you write once and use again and again: perfect for receipts. PHP runs on a SERVER, not on your phone. In this lab a small PHP practice runner in your browser runs your code, so you can learn the basics. It supports the beginner parts of PHP.
lessons.analogy: A function is your receipt machine: put in the item, the price and how many, and out comes a neat line.
steps: function receiptLine($item, $price, $qty = 1) { return ...; } The $qty = 1 is a default: if you do not give it, it is 1.
return gives the answer back. echo prints it.
number_format(1500) turns 1500 into 1,500 (nice for money).
Call your function many times with different items.
lessons.starter:
<?php
// Mission 1: function receiptLine($item, $price, $qty = 1)
//            it RETURNS text like:  Rice x2 = ₦600   (item, x, qty, = ₦, price times qty)
//            use number_format() for the money so 1500 shows as 1,500
// Mission 2: function orderTotal($price, $qty) returns $price * $qty
// Mission 3: the default! receiptLine("Yam", 50) must work and mean qty 1
// Mission 4: echo 3 receipt lines (your 3 items) and then a line "Total: ₦..."
lessons.solution:
<?php
function receiptLine($item, $price, $qty = 1) {
  return $item . " x" . $qty . " = ₦" . number_format($price * $qty);
}

function orderTotal($price, $qty) {
  return $price * $qty;
}

echo receiptLine("{{I1}}", {{P1n}}, 2) . "\n";
echo receiptLine("{{I2}}", {{P2n}}) . "\n";
echo receiptLine("{{I3}}", {{P3n}}, 3) . "\n";

$grand = orderTotal({{P1n}}, 2) + orderTotal({{P2n}}, 1) + orderTotal({{P3n}}, 3);
echo "Total: ₦" . number_format($grand) . "\n";

quiz.q: What is a default parameter, like $qty = 1?
o: A value used when you do not give one
quiz.why: If you skip it, PHP uses the default.

quiz.q: What is the difference between return and echo?
o: return gives the value back, echo prints it
quiz.why: A function can return a value so other code can use it.

quiz.q: What does number_format(1500) give?
quiz.why: It adds commas to make money easy to read.
